network.target_molecule: Tryptophan, stereochemistry unspecified; racemic formation expected
network.overall_strategy: This is a connected, conditional research network, not a validated complete prebiotic synthesis. The supplied literature does not establish even one geochemically complete route from simple feedstocks to tryptophan, much less ten. Accordingly, indole, indole-3-acetaldehyde and indole-3-pyruvic acid are explicit boundary inputs with unresolved terrestrial supplies. No unsupported conversion of indole plus acetaldehyde or pyruvate into these substituted indoles is asserted. Indole production in irradiated extraterrestrial ice supports a possible external source, not an aqueous terrestrial synthesis (Wang et al., 2024). Ten distinct directed reaction sequences are encoded: four aldehyde-processing variants, three keto-acid reductive-amination variants, two transamination variants, and one glycolaldehyde-to-serine route ending in the demonstrated pyridoxal-metal reaction. These are not ten independently established reaction families. Cyanohydrin capture is an alternative entry into Strecker chemistry, not a demonstrated additional source of the indolic aldehyde. Hydantoin processing and strong-base hydrolysis are conditional laboratory comparators; their natural operation is not established. Numerical conditions below are proposed screening windows unless explicitly identified as literature-reported, and are not claimed to reproduce unpublished experimental details. Every experiment excludes molecular oxygen. Surface reactions are locally shielded from destructive UV except the explicitly illuminated photochemical branch. Interstage separation, pH adjustment and catalyst compatibility are requirements, not assumed natural processes. Neutral formulas are bookkeeping reference states; actual protonation follows solution pH. Solid formula units are included where minerals are consumed or produced. The schema lacks a coproduct role, so terminal coproducts use intermediate. The target has environment_formed set to null because different candidate reactions form it in different environments.

reactions.name: Imine-first Strecker conversion of supplied indole-3-acetaldehyde

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8.0-9.0; aldehyde 0.1-1 mM; total ammonia 0.05-0.5 M; total cyanide 5-50 mM; 1-48 h. Locally UV-shielded. Quantify aldehyde degradation, oligomers and aminonitrile independently.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an imine or iminium species with the aldehyde; cyanide addition gives the alpha-aminonitrile. One water molecule is released per aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Standard Strecker chemistry supplies the correct carbon skeleton without an indole-ring coupling assumption. The supplied review identifies this as a candidate, not a demonstrated prebiotic tryptophan synthesis; Wang et al. (2024) establish indole formation in ice, not this aqueous conversion. Substrate-specific yield and the aldehyde's prebiotic supply remain unresolved. This is an analogue-supported, unvalidated indolic extension of established Strecker chemistry (Strecker, 1850).

reactions.name: Direct complete hydrolysis of tryptophan aminonitrile

conditions.other: Conditional laboratory screen: 0.05-0.5 M hydroxide; 1-7 days. Separate the aminonitrile-containing fraction from residual cyanide before heating. Analyze aminocarboxamide accumulation as well as tryptophan. Neutral-acid products denote a subsequent protonation workup. This alkalinity is not asserted to characterize natural vents.

reactions.mechanism: Sequential nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis consume two water equivalents and release one ammonia equivalent per tryptophan. The amide is a transient mechanistic intermediate rather than a separately supplied branch point.
reactions.reasoning: Nitrile hydrolysis is established reaction-class chemistry (Strecker, 1850), but the supplied evidence does not establish quantitative hydrolysis of this indolic aminonitrile. The stated conditions are a proposed laboratory test, not a reported yield-bearing protocol. Alkaline processing avoids assuming that acid conditions compatible with simple aminonitriles preserve an indole. Complete amide cleavage and target survival are independent bottlenecks; operation at natural pH 9-11 remains unvalidated.

reactions.name: Reversible cyanohydrin capture of supplied indole-3-acetaldehyde

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7.5-8.5; aldehyde 0.1-1 mM; total cyanide 5-50 mM; ammonia initially absent; 1-24 h. Shield from UV and measure the reversible aldehyde-cyanohydrin distribution.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the aldehyde carbonyl and protonation gives its cyanohydrin. No substitution on the indole ring or on a hydroxymethyl side chain is invoked.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative for this particular substrate under the stated conditions: the supplied research does not report its cyanohydrin. The chemically justified purpose is reversible aldehyde capture before ammonia exposure, not creation of an additional aromatic precursor. This is an alternative entry within established cyanide-carbonyl chemistry, not independent evidence for prebiotic tryptophan.

reactions.name: Ammonia trapping of the cyanohydrin equilibrium as aminonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8.0-9.0; total ammonia 0.05-0.5 M; cyanohydrin 0.1-1 mM; 1-72 h. Maintain the cyanide-containing closed system and measure aldehyde, cyanohydrin and aminonitrile together.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanohydrin dissociation releases aldehyde and cyanide. Ammonia captures aldehyde as an imine, followed by cyanide readdition. The displayed equation is the net conversion, not a claimed direct displacement of hydroxide.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative, substrate-specific entry variant. General Strecker chemistry supports the imine/cyanide sequence (Strecker, 1850), but no supplied study demonstrates productive passage through this indolic cyanohydrin. Explicit dissociation and retrapping avoid the unsupported assumption that ammonia simply substitutes an unactivated hydroxyl group. Pathways using this edge are not mechanistically independent of rxn_001.

reactions.name: Carbon-dioxide incorporation into an indolic hydantoin

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8.0-9.5; dissolved inorganic carbon 0.05-0.5 M; aminonitrile 0.1-1 mM; 1-7 days. Determine carbonate speciation and identify hydantoin against a structural standard rather than inferring it from aminonitrile loss.

reactions.mechanism: Carbamation followed by cyclization and rearrangement produces a hydantoin. Both aminonitrile nitrogen atoms are retained. Net stoichiometry is one aminonitrile plus one carbon dioxide; no net ammonia or water coproduct is required.
reactions.reasoning: Bucherer-Bergs chemistry provides a conventional synthetic precedent for converting carbonyl-derived aminonitriles into hydantoins (Bucherer and Lieb, 1934). The supplied prebiotic research does not demonstrate this indolic conversion, so its environmental application is speculative. Carbon dioxide availability alone does not establish carbamation or cyclization rates.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic opening of tryptophan hydantoin

conditions.other: Conditional laboratory screen: 0.1-1 M hydroxide; 6-72 h; isolated hydantoin feed. Determine whether N-carbamoyltryptophan accumulates before increasing residence time. These strong-base conditions are not asserted to be geochemically supplied.

reactions.mechanism: Water addition and cleavage of a hydantoin acyl-nitrogen bond open the ring to N-carbamoyltryptophan, consuming one water equivalent.
reactions.reasoning: Hydantoin hydrolysis is conventional chemistry associated with the Bucherer-Bergs synthesis, but the provided studies establish neither indolic-substrate kinetics nor natural operation of this step. Accordingly, this is a speculative prebiotic edge and a conditional laboratory comparator. Ring opening is represented separately because it does not establish subsequent removal of the carbamoyl group.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic decarbamoylation of N-carbamoyltryptophan

conditions.other: Conditional laboratory screen: 0.1-1 M hydroxide; 1-48 h with time-resolved sampling and rapid cooling of analytical samples. Quantify tryptophan formation and destruction independently. Natural pH 9-11 operation is an unresolved alternative, not an assumed equivalent.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the substituted urea functionality releases tryptophan, ammonia and carbon dioxide. In alkaline solution the latter products occur largely as ammonium/ammonia and inorganic-carbon species according to pH.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative in the requested prebiotic setting: no supplied study validates this substrate and operating window. It is an explicit bottleneck rather than an automatic consequence of hydantoin opening. Hydrothermal tryptophan degradation at substantially higher temperatures is documented by Guo et al. (2019), but that study does not establish stability or yield here. The branch fails if carbamoyl cleavage cannot outpace target destruction.

reactions.name: Ferrous-hydroxide-coupled reductive amination of indole-3-pyruvate
agents: Iron(II) hydroxide, consumed reductant rather than a catalyst

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 9.0-10.5; indolepyruvate 0.1-1 mM; total ammonia 0.05-0.5 M; fresh Fe(OH)2 slurry in excess of the two-equivalent electron-balance requirement; 1-72 h. Prepare and characterize solids without oxygen. Minimize warm storage of the keto acid.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia-derived imine reduction consumes two electrons. Per tryptophan, two Fe(OH)2 formula units are oxidized to two FeOOH formula units, with one net water coproduct. Molecular oxygen is unnecessary.
reactions.reasoning: Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003) support iron-mediated reductive amination of alpha-keto acids; Barge et al. (2019) demonstrate strong pH and iron-redox-state dependence for simpler substrates. Neither supplied result establishes indolepyruvate-to-tryptophan conversion. This substrate extension is speculative. FeOOH is an atom-balanced ferric endpoint, not an assertion that a particular active mineral phase has been identified; competing iron phases and keto-acid decomposition must be measured.

reactions.name: Pyritization-coupled reductive amination candidate
agents: Mackinawite, consumed iron-sulfide reactant and reaction interface

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8.0-9.5; indolepyruvate 0.1-1 mM; total ammonia 0.05-0.5 M; dissolved sulfide 1-10 mM; FeS slurry; 1-72 h. Establish pyrite formation and sulfur balance alongside organic-product analysis.

reactions.mechanism: The proposed net coupling oxidizes sulfide sulfur to disulfide sulfur during FeS2 formation, supplying the two electrons required for imine reduction. Iron can remain Fe(II). One FeS and one H2S are consumed per tryptophan in the displayed bookkeeping.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative coupling: Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003) provide precedent for FeS-associated reductive amination, but the supplied research does not validate this pyritization stoichiometry, electron-transfer mechanism or indolic substrate. The edge is distinguished from rxn_008 by its sulfur-based electron source. Pyrite precipitation by itself would not demonstrate reduction of the organic imine.

reactions.name: Pyrite-photocatalytic reductive amination with formate oxidation
agents: Natural pyrite as a separately supplied heterogeneous photocatalyst

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8.0-9.0; indolepyruvate 0.1-1 mM; total ammonia 0.02-0.1 M; formate 0.02-0.1 M; pyrite 0.1-1 g/L; selected 365-450 nm illumination at 1-10 mW/cm2. Include dark, mineral-free and donor-free controls. The illumination window is a laboratory test, not an established natural filter.

reactions.mechanism: Photoexcited pyrite mediates reduction of an ammonia-derived imine while formate oxidation supplies two electrons and produces carbon dioxide. Water is the other net coproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Li et al. (2024) demonstrate pyrite-photocatalytic alpha-keto-acid amination, including low-yield phenylalanine formation from an aromatic substrate. That is analogue evidence, not demonstration for indolepyruvate. The stated formate coupling and illumination recipe are proposed and are not attributed to that paper as verified conditions. Indole photolysis, catalyst corrosion and unproductive charge recombination are competing processes.

reactions.name: Glycine-to-indolepyruvate nonenzymatic transamination candidate
agents: Fe2+ coordinated by the amino-acid and keto-acid substrates

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 6.5-7.5; indolepyruvate 0.1-1 mM; glycine 0.05-0.2 M; total added Fe2+ 10-100 micromolar; 1-7 days. Measure dissolved iron and precipitates; avoid phosphate and sulfide in the initial mechanistic test. Shield from UV.

reactions.mechanism: A metal-chelated imine between the amino donor and keto acceptor undergoes proton transfer and hydrolysis, transferring the amino group from glycine to indolepyruvate. Glyoxylate is the stoichiometric coproduct; no external reductant is required.
reactions.reasoning: Nonenzymatic transamination has reaction-class support, including Ter-Ovanessian et al. (2025), but the supplied research does not demonstrate this donor-acceptor pair or these Fe2+ conditions. This is therefore speculative. Fe2+ is selected for availability and chelation chemistry, not presumed PLP-equivalent activity. Slow proton transfer, equilibrium limitations and indolepyruvate decay may eliminate measurable target flux.

reactions.name: Alanine-to-indolepyruvate nonenzymatic transamination candidate
agents: Fe2+ coordinated by the amino-acid and keto-acid substrates

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 6.5-7.5; indolepyruvate 0.1-1 mM; alanine 0.05-0.2 M; total added Fe2+ 10-100 micromolar; 1-7 days. Use conditions matched to rxn_011 and assay both pyruvate and tryptophan. Shield from UV.

reactions.mechanism: Metal-assisted imine formation, proton redistribution and hydrolysis transfer the amino group from alanine to indolepyruvate, producing pyruvate and tryptophan.
reactions.reasoning: Ter-Ovanessian et al. (2025) support nonenzymatic amino-transfer chemistry in general, not this specific pair. The edge is speculative and does not inherit a demonstrated yield from biological aminotransferases. Alanine is a chemically distinct donor with a different keto-acid coproduct, but no intrinsic advantage over glycine is assumed. Donor excess alone cannot establish favorable equilibrium or useful kinetics.

reactions.name: Pyridoxal-metal-mediated replacement of serine hydroxyl by indole
agents: Cu2+ as a laboratory metal-ion co-catalyst

conditions.other: The supplied report describes approximately 373 K model chemistry. Proposed screening brackets, not a transcription of the original recipe: pH 7-9; serine 10-100 mM; indole 1-10 mM; pyridoxal 0.1-1 mM; Cu2+ 0.01-0.1 mM; 1-24 h. Use cyanide-free, sulfide-free, desalted serine feed. Exact catalyst formulation must be checked against the primary protocol before claiming replication.

reactions.mechanism: Serine forms a pyridoxal Schiff base. Dehydration generates a catalyst-bound aminoacrylate equivalent; indole attacks at its beta carbon, and hydrolysis releases tryptophan while regenerating the aldehyde cofactor. Net stoichiometry is indole plus serine to tryptophan plus water.
reactions.reasoning: This is the strongest substrate-specific nonenzymatic precedent: Metzler, Ikawa and Snell (1954), discussed by Newton and Snell (1964), report tryptophan formation from indole and serine with pyridoxal-metal catalysts. Nevertheless, the supplied summary does not establish the exact numerical recipe above. Pyridoxal supply and persistent soluble Cu2+ are not established under reducing prebiotic conditions. This is a conditional laboratory benchmark, not a metal-only or cofactor-free prebiotic solution.

reactions.name: Glycolaldehyde Strecker synthesis of serine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8.0-9.0; glycolaldehyde 1-10 mM; total ammonia 0.05-0.5 M; total cyanide 5-50 mM; 1-48 h. Shield from UV during aminonitrile accumulation. Quantify cyanohydrin and sugar-derived side products.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia condenses at glycolaldehyde's aldehyde group, followed by cyanide addition. The hydroxymethyl group is retained, giving the serine carbon skeleton and one water coproduct.
reactions.reasoning: This is a conventional Strecker connection from a chemically appropriate C2 aldehyde to a C3 amino-acid precursor. The supplied review identifies glycolaldehyde-derived Strecker chemistry as a serine source; cyanosulfidic work independently supports access to relevant small aldehydes (Patel et al., 2015). Those precedents do not validate the proposed concentrations or integrated tryptophan production. Unlike an indole-side-chain substitution proposal, the required connectivity follows directly from carbonyl addition.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of serine aminonitrile and preparation of a compatible serine feed

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 1-2; 1-14 days. Use an aminonitrile fraction already separated from free cyanide. Track the aminoamide intermediate and serine loss. Before rxn_013, cool, adjust to pH 7-8 and desalt; verify removal of cyanide and other Cu-binding contaminants. These conditioning operations are external requirements, not demonstrated natural separations.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydration followed by aminoamide hydrolysis consumes two water equivalents and releases one ammonia equivalent per serine. The ammonia is predominantly protonated under the reaction conditions.
reactions.reasoning: Aminonitrile hydrolysis completes the conventional Strecker serine module (Strecker, 1850, reaction-class precedent). The supplied report supports this module conceptually but provides no substrate-specific rate at the proposed pH and temperature. Its connection to the Metzler, Ikawa and Snell (1954) reaction is conditional on demonstrated serine recovery and solution conditioning; residual cyanide could suppress or alter the metal-cofactor chemistry.

pathways.name: Imine-first indolic Strecker followed by direct hydrolysis
pathways.description: From externally supplied indole-3-acetaldehyde, form the aminonitrile and hydrolyze it directly. Correct connectivity is supported by reaction-class chemistry, but neither precursor availability nor substrate-specific integrated yield is established.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin-first indolic Strecker followed by direct hydrolysis
pathways.description: Capture the supplied aldehyde reversibly as a cyanohydrin, then introduce ammonia and hydrolyze the resulting aminonitrile. This is a distinct directed sequence within the same Strecker family, not an independent solution to aldehyde sourcing.

pathways.name: Imine-first Strecker followed by hydantoin processing
pathways.description: Divert the aminonitrile into a hydantoin, open its ring and remove the carbamoyl group. This conventional synthetic concept is a conditional laboratory comparator; the indolic cyclization and two hydrolysis stages require independent validation.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin-first capture followed by hydantoin processing
pathways.description: Combine the alternative aldehyde-capture sequence with hydantoin formation and processing. This is the fourth aldehyde-family graph sequence, not a fourth independent prebiotic mechanism. It retains the cyanohydrin-equilibrium and hydantoin-hydrolysis uncertainties.

pathways.name: Ferrous-hydroxide-driven keto-acid reductive amination
pathways.description: Use supplied indole-3-pyruvic acid and ammonia, with stoichiometric Fe(II) oxidation providing reducing equivalents. Analogue-supported but unvalidated for this keto acid; neither its formation nor the identity of the ferric product is presumed established.

pathways.name: Sulfur-oxidation-driven keto-acid reductive amination
pathways.description: Test coupling of indolepyruvate amination to FeS/H2S conversion into pyrite. This explicitly balanced sulfur-redox hypothesis requires demonstration of both electron transfer to the organic substrate and productive mineral conversion.

pathways.name: Formate-fed pyrite photoredox reductive amination
pathways.description: Use pyrite-mediated photochemistry and formate oxidation to reduce an ammonia-derived indolepyruvate imine. Aromatic-keto-acid analogues motivate the test, but indolic photostability, donor compatibility and target yield are unresolved.

pathways.name: Glycine-donor transamination
pathways.description: Transfer an amino group from glycine to supplied indolepyruvate, yielding glyoxylate as coproduct. This is a redox-neutral, metal-assisted candidate without substrate-specific experimental validation in the supplied evidence.

pathways.name: Alanine-donor transamination
pathways.description: Transfer an amino group from alanine to supplied indolepyruvate, yielding pyruvate as coproduct. This donor-distinct alternative requires its own kinetic and equilibrium assessment and is not presumed superior to glycine.

pathways.name: Glycolaldehyde-to-serine module feeding the pyridoxal-metal benchmark
pathways.description: Generate serine through glycolaldehyde Strecker chemistry and aminonitrile hydrolysis, condition the serine-containing fraction, then couple it with boundary-supplied indole using the nonenzymatic pyridoxal-metal model. The terminal reaction has direct precedent; precursor recovery, interstage compatibility and prebiotic cofactor availability are not established.

evaluation.target_molecule: Tryptophan, stereochemistry unspecified; racemic formation expected

pathway_evaluations.feedback: A chemically credible conditional route from supplied indole-3-acetaldehyde. General Strecker chemistry supports rxn_001, and complete aminonitrile hydrolysis can produce tryptophan. However, substrate-specific yields, hydrolysis conditions and product-survival measurements are not supplied. A Hydrothermal label alone does not establish a suitable hydrolysis window. The scarcity of tryptophan in discharge inventories does not invalidate Strecker chemistry using a supplied indolic aldehyde.
suggestions: Specify pH, temperature, concentrations and residence times for both reactions.
Demonstrate complete nitrile hydrolysis rather than accumulation of the corresponding amide, while measuring tryptophan recovery and degradation.
Define the physical transfer and solution adjustment between Strecker formation and hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyanohydrin formation is plausible, and rxn_004 is appropriately described as trapping an equilibrium rather than direct displacement of an unactivated hydroxyl group. Its effectiveness depends on aldehyde release, imine formation and competing cyanohydrin stability. This is an alternative entry into the same Strecker route, not independent evidence for aldehyde supply or target formation. The final hydrolysis has the same unresolved operating requirements as P1.
suggestions: Measure cyanohydrin, free aldehyde and aminonitrile concentrations during ammonia addition.
Establish an ammonia/cyanide/pH window that favors aminonitrile accumulation.
Validate the hydrolysis and transfer procedure using the actual cyanohydrin-processing mixture.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The hydantoin and N-carbamoyltryptophan intermediates form a coherent, conserved route. Bucherer–Bergs-type chemistry supports considering rxn_005, but the supplied research does not establish this indolic implementation. Hydantoin opening and decarbamoylation are credible laboratory transformations, yet water in a net equation does not establish useful uncatalyzed rates. The acknowledged strong-base comparator is not accompanied by operating conditions or a natural environmental justification.
suggestions: Provide substrate-specific evidence for hydantoin formation and identify the product structurally.
Specify base identity, concentration, temperature and duration separately for ring opening and decarbamoylation.
Measure conversion, tryptophan survival and competing reactions across the complete hydantoin-processing sequence.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a valid directed combination of cyanohydrin-mediated Strecker entry and hydantoin processing. Its principal limitations are the unmeasured cyanohydrin-to-aminonitrile equilibrium and the unspecified conditions for hydantoin hydrolysis and decarbamoylation. The pathway is not penalized for its length; confidence is limited by those particular chemical and environmental uncertainties.
suggestions: Test whether the cyanohydrin-processing mixture supports subsequent hydantoin formation without an assumed purification.
Track aminonitrile, hydantoin and N-carbamoyltryptophan rather than relying only on a final amino-acid signal.
Define the required separation and pH adjustments, distinguishing laboratory operations from physically justified environmental processes.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The balanced reaction supplies the required two-electron reduction through oxidation of two Fe(II) centers; molecular oxygen is not required. Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003) and Barge et al. (2019) provide relevant keto-acid analogues, but the supplied findings do not demonstrate indole-3-pyruvate conversion. Mineral phase, pH-dependent reactivity, competing carbonyl reduction and substrate instability remain unresolved.
suggestions: Specify and characterize the initial iron phase, Fe(II)/Fe(III) ratio, pH and temperature rather than treating different iron systems as interchangeable.
Measure tryptophan alongside unreacted indole-3-pyruvate, hydroxy-acid products and decomposition products.
Correlate amino-acid formation with iron oxidation and mineral transformation using appropriate mineral-free and ammonia-free controls.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The FeS/H2S-to-pyrite stoichiometry can formally provide the reducing equivalents required for reductive amination, so there is no conservation violation. Nevertheless, favorable pyritization does not establish kinetic coupling to the indolic imine. The cited FeS-based keto-acid chemistry is relevant precedent, not direct evidence for this particular sulfur-oxidation mechanism or substrate.
suggestions: Demonstrate coupled pyrite formation and tryptophan production under the same defined conditions.
Determine whether reduction involves transferable surface electrons, generated hydrogen or another intermediate.
Include FeS-only, sulfide-only and no-ammonia controls, and quantify competing sulfide reactions and substrate loss.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Formate oxidation supplies a balanced two-electron source, and Li et al. (2024) provide relevant pyrite-photocatalytic keto-acid reductive-amination precedent. However, the supplied findings do not establish this formate-fed indole-3-pyruvate system. The photon spectrum, catalyst loading and competition between productive photochemistry and indolic photodegradation are unspecified. Pyrite is named as a catalyst but its availability in this surface branch is not operationally defined.
suggestions: Specify whether mol_016 is supplied as a surface mineral or transferred from rxn_009, and record its catalytic loading and surface characteristics.
Define wavelength, photon flux, pH, ammonia concentration and formate concentration.
Use dark, no-pyrite and no-formate controls and independently measure photochemical substrate and product degradation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The amino-group transfer and glyoxylate coproduct are stoichiometrically coherent. General nonenzymatic transamination literature, including the supplied 2025 study and metal-catalysis review, supports investigation but does not demonstrate this donor–acceptor pair. No catalyst or sufficiently specific thermal regime is assigned to rxn_011, and useful net conversion cannot be inferred from analogy to enzymatic transamination.
suggestions: Specify an experimentally supported nonenzymatic catalyst and its concentration, pH and temperature window.
Measure both tryptophan and glyoxylate to establish paired transamination rather than nonspecific substrate disappearance.
Determine equilibrium limitations and whether any proposed product-removal mechanism is physically realizable.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Alanine-to-indolepyruvate transamination is balanced and identifies the correct pyruvate coproduct. Its implementation remains conditional because catalyst identity, kinetics and equilibrium behavior are not specified, and the supplied literature does not establish this substrate pair. There is insufficient evidence to rank alanine above or below glycine as the donor in this network.
suggestions: Provide catalyst-specific evidence or directly test alanine transfer to indole-3-pyruvate under defined conditions.
Quantify tryptophan and pyruvate together, including reverse-reaction controls.
Compare glycine and alanine donors under matched conditions rather than assuming donor equivalence or superiority.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway has the strongest target-specific experimental precedent: Metzler, Ikawa and Snell (1954; doi:10.1021/ja01632a004) support pyridoxal–metal-mediated tryptophan formation from serine and indole. Glycolaldehyde Strecker chemistry provides a plausible upstream serine module. The remaining deficiencies concern implementation: serine hydrolysis and recovery, removal of cyanide or other catalyst-incompatible components, and explicit pyridoxal/metal supply and conditions. The benchmark's chemical validity does not establish a naturally supplied prebiotic catalyst system.
suggestions: Record pyridoxal and the selected metal as required catalytic resources, with concentrations and literature-linked operating conditions.
Validate serine recovery and establish acceptable residual cyanide, ammonia and salt concentrations before coupling.
Demonstrate the complete sequence using serine produced by rxn_014 and rxn_015 rather than substituting purified commercial serine.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally valid: all 25 molecule nodes and 15 reaction nodes participate in a connected graph, IDs are consistent, and the ten listed sequences reach mol_025. The deterministic check establishes conservation for every reaction; none is UNBALANCED. Make the small coefficients explicit: rxn_002 and rxn_015 consume 2 H2O, while rxn_008 consumes 2 Fe(OH)2 and produces 2 FeOOH. These are bookkeeping corrections, not conservation failures. Literature alignment is good in its restraint: the network acknowledges unresolved boundary supplies, distinguishes analogue evidence from target-specific evidence, and avoids unsupported indole side-chain construction. Accepting declared starting materials is not itself a validity defect, although their unresolved provenance limits claims of geochemical completeness. The main weakness is operational specification: the numerical screening windows mentioned in the strategy are absent from the reaction entries, and catalyst loadings, residence times, transfer mechanisms and compatibility tests are largely unspecified. Anoxia and selective UV shielding are sensible constraints but do not resolve these omissions. Reaction-level citations and evidence grades should also be added. P10 has the strongest demonstrated final transformation; the mineral-redox, photoredox and transamination branches remain substrate-specific research hypotheses. Overall confidence reflects the chemistry and shared implementation bottlenecks, not pathway counts, shared-node counts or environment ordering. This is a useful conditional research network, but it is not approved at the required network confidence threshold of 0.9.
